HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: the head & neck packs airway, vessels, nerves & glands into a tiny space — so the clinical anatomy is dense & high-yield: facial palsy, neck lumps, thyroid surgery, salivary stones, airway emergencies and head injury. This subtab ties it together into the scenarios you’ll be examined on.
Facial Nerve Palsy — UMN vs LMN
The key distinction
  • LMN lesion (Bell’s palsy, CN VII itself) → weakness of the WHOLE ipsilateral face, including the forehead
  • UMN lesion (stroke) → forehead SPARED (the upper face has bilateral cortical input)
CN VII beyond movement
  • Also carries taste (anterior ⅔ tongue via chorda tympani), supplies stapedius (→ hyperacusis) & drives lacrimation/salivation
  • Five branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical (“Two Zebras Bit My Coat”)
Neck Lumps & the Triangles
Midline lumps
  • Thyroglossal cyst — moves up on swallowing AND tongue protrusion (tethered to the foramen caecum); at/below the hyoid
  • Thyroid masses (goitre/nodule) move with swallowing but not tongue protrusion
Lateral lumps
  • Branchial cyst — anterior to the upper ⅓ of sternocleidomastoid (2nd branchial cleft remnant); young adults
  • Lymphadenopathy (infection/lymphoma/metastasis); Virchow’s node (left supraclavicular) = gastric cancer
  • Cystic hygroma, carotid body tumour (pulsatile, at the bifurcation)
Thyroid & Parathyroid Surgery
Nerves at risk
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve — in the tracheo-oesophageal groove near the inferior thyroid artery; injury → hoarse voice (vocal cord palsy); bilateral injury → airway obstruction
  • External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve — near the superior thyroid artery; injury → weak, tiring voice (can’t sing high — cricothyroid)
Parathyroids
  • Four glands behind the thyroid; inadvertent removal → hypocalcaemia (perioral tingling, Chvostek’s & Trousseau’s signs, tetany)
The Salivary Glands
Parotid
  • The facial nerve (CN VII) runs through it (dividing it into lobes) — a parotid tumour or surgery can cause facial palsy
  • Secretomotor supply is CN IX (glossopharyngeal, via the otic ganglion); its duct (Stensen’s) opens opposite the 2nd upper molar; mumps causes painful swelling
Submandibular
  • Drains via Wharton’s duct into the floor of the mouth; the commonest site of salivary stones (mixed, viscous saliva)
  • A stone → painful swelling at mealtimes
Airway Emergencies
Cricothyroidotomy
  • Emergency airway through the cricothyroid membrane (between the thyroid & cricoid cartilages) — a quick, superficial, relatively avascular route
Tracheostomy
  • A planned airway through the 2nd–4th tracheal rings (below the thyroid isthmus)
  • The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring — the landmark for cricoid pressure
The Scalp & Head Injury
The scalp (SCALP)
  • Skin · Connective tissue (dense, vascular) · Aponeurosis (epicranius) · Loose areolar tissue · Pericranium
  • Wounds bleed profusely (vessels held open by the dense connective tissue)
  • The loose areolar layer is the “dangerous area” — infection spreads here & can reach the cranial venous sinuses via emissary veins (→ meningitis)
Intracranial bleeds
  • Extradural — middle meningeal artery at the pterion (thin bone); a lucid interval then decline; lens (biconvex) shape
  • Subdural — torn bridging veins (elderly/alcoholics); crescent shape; slower
Ear, Eye & the Cavernous Sinus
Otitis media / mastoiditis — middle-ear infection can spread to the mastoid air cells; the facial nerve runs nearby.
Conductive vs sensorineural — Rinne & Weber tests localise the hearing loss.
CN III palsy — “down & out” eye, ptosis, fixed dilated pupil (a surgical CN III = aneurysm/uncal herniation).
Horner’s syndrome — ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis (sympathetic chain — Pancoast tumour, carotid dissection).
Cavernous sinus — carries CN III, IV, V1, V2 & VI + the internal carotid; thrombosis (facial infection via the ophthalmic veins) threatens them all.
Vessels & Lymphatics of the Neck
Common carotid bifurcates at ~C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage) into internal & external carotids.
Carotid sinus (baroreceptor, CN IX) & carotid body (chemoreceptor) sit at the bifurcation.
Internal jugular vein — the target for central venous access (lateral to the carotid).
Cervical lymph nodes (levels I–VI) — mapped for staging head & neck cancer; deep cervical nodes drain most of the region.
🧠 Mnemonics
Facial nerve branches — “Two Zebras Bit My Coat”: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical.
Forehead spared = UMN; forehead involved = LMN (Bell’s palsy).
Scalp = SCALP: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar (dangerous), Pericranium.
Thyroglossal cyst moves on tongue protrusion; thyroid moves on swallowing only.
⭐ Exam Pearls
LMN (Bell’s) facial palsy involves the forehead; UMN (stroke) spares it.
Thyroglossal cyst rises on tongue protrusion & swallowing (foramen caecum tract).
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (thyroid surgery) → hoarse voice; bilateral → airway obstruction.
External laryngeal nerve (near the superior thyroid artery) → weak/tiring voice.
Parathyroid damage → hypocalcaemia (Chvostek’s & Trousseau’s signs).
The facial nerve runs through the parotid; parotid pathology can cause facial palsy.
Submandibular gland (Wharton’s duct) is the commonest site of salivary stones.
Cricothyroidotomy = cricothyroid membrane; tracheostomy = 2nd–4th tracheal rings.
Extradural = middle meningeal artery at the pterion (lucid interval); subdural = bridging veins.
Cavernous sinus contains CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI + the internal carotid.
